samf-senior-2011-r2-02.title: Through the middle point
samf-senior-2011-r2-02.body:
There are 2 ways to go from $A$ to the common corner of the two squares (right then up, or up then right) and 2 ways from there to $B$. Total $2\times2=4$.

**Answer: (A) 4**

samf-senior-2011-r2-03.title: Make the piles as equal as possible
samf-senior-2011-r2-03.body:
If the largest pile has $n$ coins, the four piles contain at most $n+(n-1)+(n-2)+(n-3)=4n-6$ coins. We need $4n-6\ge15$, so $n\ge5.25$ and $n\ge6$. With 6 it works: $6+4+3+2=15$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

samf-senior-2011-r2-04.title: Maximise top, minimise bottom
samf-senior-2011-r2-04.body:
To make the fraction large we want $M+N$ large and $M-N$ a small positive number. The smallest positive value of $M-N$ is 1, and then $M+N$ is largest for $M=50,N=49$, giving $\frac{99}{1}=99$. (Any pair with $M-N\ge2$ gives at most $\frac{99}{2}$, and a negative value is worse.)

**Answer: (B) 99**

samf-senior-2011-r2-05.title: One can of each
samf-senior-2011-r2-05.body:
One can of orange contains $\frac25$ can of yellow and one can of green contains $\frac13$ can of yellow. Mixing one can of each gives $\frac25+\frac13=\frac{11}{15}$ can of yellow in 2 cans, i.e. $\frac{11}{30}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{11}{30}$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-06.title: Groups of 13
samf-senior-2011-r2-06.body:
A group of 12 guests needs one waiter, so each 13 people serve 12 guests. $400=30\times13+10$: 30 full groups serve $360$ guests, and the remaining 10 places can hold 1 more waiter and 9 more guests. With $31$ waiters the guests are $400-31=369\le12\cdot31=372$, fine. With 32 waiters there would be only 368 guests. So the maximum is 369.

**Answer: (C) 369**

samf-senior-2011-r2-07.title: Pythagoras
samf-senior-2011-r2-07.body:
Let the radii be $R>r$. The tangent chord $ST$ touches the small circle at its midpoint, so by Pythagoras $R^2-r^2=20^2=400$. The shaded area is $\pi R^2-\pi r^2=400\pi$.

**Answer: (E) $400\pi$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-07.title: Shrink the inner circle
samf-senior-2011-r2-07.body:
The area does not depend on the radii (only on $ST$), so let $r\to0$: then $ST$ is a diameter of the large circle, $R=20$, and the area is $\pi\cdot20^2=400\pi$.

**Answer: (E)**

samf-senior-2011-r2-08.title: Prime factorisation
samf-senior-2011-r2-08.body:
$10\,000=2^4\cdot5^4$. If a factor contained both 2 and 5 it would be a multiple of 10 and end in 0. So one factor is $2^4=16$ and the other $5^4=625$ and their sum is $641$.

**Answer: (A) 641**

samf-senior-2011-r2-09.title: Table of sums
samf-senior-2011-r2-09.body:
The faces are $1,1,2,3,5,8$; there are 36 equally likely ordered outcomes. Counting those whose sum is in $\{2,3,5,8,13,21\}$: sum 2 ($1+1$): $2\cdot2=4$ outcomes; sum 3 ($1+2$ or $2+1$): $2\cdot1\cdot2=4$; sum 5 ($2+3$ or $3+2$): 2; sum 8 ($3+5$ or $5+3$): 2; sum 13 ($5+8$ or $8+5$): 2. That is $4+4+2+2+2=14$ outcomes, so the probability is $\frac{14}{36}=\frac7{18}$.

**Answer: (B) $\frac7{18}$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-10.title: Pair the factors
samf-senior-2011-r2-10.body:
Pair $17\cdot23$, $18\cdot22$, $19\cdot21$: $(20-n)(20+n)=400-n^2$, which is about $400$ for $n=1,2,3$ (the exact values are $391,396,399$). So the product is about $400^3\cdot20=20^7=1.28\times10^9$ (actually $1.24\times10^9$). The closest power of 10 is $10^9$.

**Answer: (D) $10^9$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-11.title: Area bookkeeping
samf-senior-2011-r2-11.body:
Let $C$ be the area of the circle, $S$ that of the square and $F$ the area of one flap. Then $C-S=4F$. The shaded region is the square with the four folded flaps removed, so its area is $S-4F=S-(C-S)=2S-C$. The diagonal of the square is the diameter 2, so its side is $\sqrt2$ and $S=2$. Hence the shaded area is $2\cdot2-\pi=4-\pi$.

**Answer: (D) $4-\pi$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-12.title: Difference of squares
samf-senior-2011-r2-12.body:
$(M-N)(M+N)=2011$, and 2011 is prime (it is not divisible by any prime up to 43). So $M-N=1$ and $M+N=2011$, giving $M=1006$ and $N=1005$.

**Answer: (B) 1005**

samf-senior-2011-r2-14.title: Coordinates
samf-senior-2011-r2-14.body:
Put the square as $[0,14]^2$. The small circles touch the top corners: centres $(3,11)$ and $(11,11)$. The large circle touches the bottom and is centred on the axis of symmetry: centre $(7,R)$. It touches a small circle: $(7-3)^2+(11-R)^2=(R+3)^2$, so $16+121-22R=6R+9$, $28R=128$ and $R=\frac{32}7$.

**Answer: (E) $\frac{32}7$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-15.title: Substitute t = 3^x
samf-senior-2011-r2-15.body:
With $t=3^x>0$ we have $9^x=t^2$, so the expression is $t-t^2=\frac14-\left(t-\frac12\right)^2\le\frac14$, with equality at $t=\frac12$ (attainable, since $3^x=\frac12$ has a solution).

**Answer: (A) $\frac14$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-16.title: Write each as a reciprocal of a sum of roots
samf-senior-2011-r2-16.body:
Rationalising: $\sqrt{11}-\sqrt{10}=\frac1{\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{10}}$ and $\sqrt{10}-3=\frac1{\sqrt{10}+\sqrt9}$. Also $\frac16=\frac1{\sqrt9+\sqrt9}$, $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{20}=\frac1{2\sqrt{10}}=\frac1{\sqrt{10}+\sqrt{10}}$ and $\frac{\sqrt{11}}{22}=\frac1{\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{11}}$. Comparing the denominators $\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{11}>\sqrt{11}+\sqrt{10}>\sqrt{10}+\sqrt{10}>\sqrt{10}+\sqrt9>\sqrt9+\sqrt9$ gives, from smallest to largest, $\frac{\sqrt{11}}{22}<\sqrt{11}-\sqrt{10}<\frac{\sqrt{10}}{20}<\sqrt{10}-3<\frac16$. The middle one is $\frac{\sqrt{10}}{20}$.

**Answer: (D)**

samf-senior-2011-r2-17.title: Walk around the star
samf-senior-2011-r2-17.body:
Walk along all the lines of the star until you return to the start facing the original direction. At each of the 7 vertices you turn through $180^\circ-\theta_i$, where $\theta_i$ is the tip angle. Going around the middle region you encircled the centre 3 times, so the total turning is $3\times360^\circ$. Hence $7\cdot180^\circ-\sum\theta_i=3\cdot360^\circ$ and $\sum\theta_i=1260^\circ-1080^\circ=180^\circ$.

**Answer: (D) $180^\circ$**

samf-senior-2011-r2-17.title: Slide the lines
samf-senior-2011-r2-17.body:
Translate every line parallel to itself so that all seven pass through one point. The seven tip angles then fit side by side around that point and together fill half a revolution, so their sum is $180^\circ$.

**Answer: (D)**

samf-senior-2011-r2-18.title: Use the river's frame of reference
samf-senior-2011-r2-18.body:
In a frame moving with the water the goggles are at rest and James swims at constant speed relative to them. He swims away for 10 minutes and so needs another 10 minutes to come back. The goggles therefore drifted for $20$ minutes, covering $500$ m: $0.5$ km in $\frac13$ h, i.e. $1.5$ km/h. This is the river's speed.

**Answer: (C) 1.5 km/h**

samf-senior-2011-r2-18.title: Frame fixed to the bank
samf-senior-2011-r2-18.body:
Let James's speed in still water be $J$ and the river's speed $R$ (km/h). After $\frac16$ h he is $\frac{J-R}6$ km upstream of the loss point and the goggles are $\frac R6$ km downstream, so they are $\frac J6$ km apart. When he turns he swims downstream at $J+R$ while the goggles drift at $R$, closing the gap at $J$ km/h, which takes $\frac{J/6}J=\frac16$ h. So the goggles drifted for $\frac13$ h in total, covering $0.5$ km: $R=\frac{0.5}{1/3}=1.5$ km/h, whatever $J$ is.

**Answer: (C)**

samf-senior-2011-r2-19.title: Count the points
samf-senior-2011-r2-19.body:
Each game gives exactly 1 point in total. The winner has $4\frac12$ points, so played at least 5 games, so there were at least $6$ players. With $n$ players there are $\frac{n(n-1)}2$ points in all. The top four have $4\frac12+3\frac12+3+1\frac12=12\frac12$ points, so the other $n-4$ players share $\frac{n(n-1)}2-12\frac12$ points, and each has at most $1\frac12$. So $\frac{n(n-1)-25}2\le\frac32(n-4)$, i.e. $n^2-4n-13\le0$, so $n\le2+\sqrt{17}<6.2$, hence $n=6$. The bottom two then share $15-12\frac12=2\frac12$ points, each at most $1\frac12$, so they have $1\frac12$ and $1$. The lowest score is $1$.

**Answer: (B) 1**

samf-senior-2011-r2-20.title: Identify the people by their counts
samf-senior-2011-r2-20.body:
Nobody can shake more than 6 hands (not their own or their partner's), so the seven answers are exactly $0,1,\dots,6$. Call the person who shook $k$ hands $P_k$.

- $P_6$ shook hands with everybody except his or her partner, so everyone else has shaken at least one hand; hence the partner of $P_6$ is $P_0$.
- $P_1$ shook only $P_6$'s hand. $P_5$ shook 5 hands, not with $P_0$ (who shook none) and not with $P_1$ (whose only handshake was with $P_6$), so $P_5$'s partner is $P_1$ and $P_5$ shook hands with $P_6,P_4,P_3,P_2$ and me.
- $P_2$ shook only $P_6$ and $P_5$. $P_4$ shook 4 hands, not with $P_0$, $P_1$ or $P_2$, so $P_4$'s partner is $P_2$ and $P_4$ shook hands with $P_6,P_5,P_3$ and me.
- The remaining person $P_3$ is my partner. I shook hands with $P_6$ (everyone but $P_0$ did), $P_5$ and $P_4$, and with nobody else, so I shook 3 hands (as did $P_3$).

**Answer: (D) 3**
